title: Close Calls
statement: A weather office logged one integer temperature reading per station. Two stations make a close call when their readings differ by at most tolerance. Count the pairs of positions i < j that make a close call. Stations with equal readings are still separate stations, so equal readings form a pair too.

examples.explanation: The close calls are the two 3s, 9 with 11, 11 with 12, and 12 with 14. Pairs such as 9 and 12 differ by 3 and do not count, so the answer is 4.
All three readings are equal, so each of the 3 position pairs is a close call even with tolerance 0.

hints.content: Does the order in which the stations were logged change whether two particular stations make a close call?
If you sort the readings, the partners of a reading that are within tolerance form one unbroken stretch directly below it in the sorted order.
Sweep a right pointer across the sorted array and keep a left pointer on the smallest reading that is still within tolerance of the right one.

The left pointer never has to move backward, because the next right reading is at least as large as the current one. For each right position, the new pairs are exactly the positions from left up to just before right.
Total cost is the sort plus one pass: O(n log n) time. Checking every pair is about 112 million comparisons for 15,000 readings.

testCases.explanation: Four close calls among seven stations.
Equal readings pair up at tolerance 0.
A single station has no partner.
The widest allowed gap is exactly the tolerance.
A gap one larger than the tolerance is not a close call.
A small random batch with a moderate tolerance.
The largest input with every reading equal: every pair counts, over 112 million of them.
The largest input with random readings and a narrow tolerance.
The largest input where the whole range fits inside the tolerance.
The largest input packed into a narrow band, so many pairs just miss the tolerance.

solutions.title: Compare every pair
solutions.intuition: Look at all pairs of stations and count those whose readings differ by at most tolerance.
solutions.approach: Two nested loops over i < j, incrementing the answer when the absolute difference is at most tolerance.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n^2), about 112 million pair checks at n = 15,000
commonMistakes: Counting each pair twice by letting j start at 0.
Using a strict inequality and dropping pairs that differ by exactly the tolerance.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Checking every pair is obviously correct and is the baseline to state first. At 15,000 stations it performs over 100 million comparisons, which is why a sorted two-pointer pass is needed.

steps.title: Pair up
steps.content: In [14, 3, 9, 11, 3, 12, 20] with tolerance 2, the pair of 3s, 9 and 11, 11 and 12, and 12 and 14 pass the test.

steps.title: Total
steps.content: All other pairs differ by more than 2, so the count is 4.

solutions.title: Sort, then slide a left pointer
solutions.intuition: In sorted order, the readings within tolerance below a given reading are one contiguous block ending right before it.
solutions.approach: Sort a copy of the readings. For each right index, advance left while sorted[right] - sorted[left] exceeds tolerance. Every index from left to right - 1 pairs with right, so add right - left.
solutions.pseudocode:
sort(readings)
left = 0; pairs = 0
for right in 0..n-1:
  while readings[right] - readings[left] > tolerance: left += 1
  pairs += right - left
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the sweep
commonMistakes: Sorting with the default JavaScript sort on a normal array, which compares as strings and puts 100 before 99.
Adding right - left + 1, which counts a reading paired with itself.
Moving left back after it has advanced.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Sorting turns the pair condition into a range condition: for a fixed reading, partners within tolerance are an unbroken stretch just below it. Because readings only increase along the sweep, the left boundary moves only forward, so the sweep is linear after the O(n log n) sort. A typed array sort compares numerically. Because every reading is at most 999, a counting array plus prefix sums over the 1,000 possible values would also work in O(n + 1000); the sorted two-pointer sweep is the version that does not rely on that small range.

steps.title: Sweep
steps.content: The second 3 adds 1, 9 adds 0, 11 adds 1, 12 adds 1 (11 only), 14 adds 1 (12 only) and 20 adds 0, giving 4.
